whisper_segs.text: Good morning. It's 7 o'clock. It's Tuesday, February 24th. You're welcome to Morning Ireland.
Justin McCarthy and Audrey Carville with you till 9.
Coming up, a government U-turn on SNAs, European disunity, Hungary blocks further sanctions
on Russia. Also, Peter Mandelson released on bail, enhancing maritime security and the
online junk food ads being targeted at children.
In business, more tariff uncertainty for Irish exporters and the number of mortgage approvals
plunged in January.
And coming up in sport, Dundalk score late to draw with Rovers in Tallaght and Manchester
United grind out a win at Everton in the Premier League.
We're live on RT Radio 1, the RT Radio app and the News Channel. Your news is read this
morning by Susan Jackson.
The Minister for Education, Hildegard Nocton, and the Minister of State for Special Education,
Michael Moynihan, have confirmed there will be no reductions to special needs assistance
for the next school year and all schools due to get additional SNAs will receive them.
An extra 19 million euro is to be provided to the Department of Education and Youth to
fund the changed approach following a meeting of government party leaders and several ministers
last night. Our education correspondent Emma O'Kelly reports.
This is welcome news for the 194 schools that were due to lose SNAs next year following
reviews of their allocation. It comes ahead of protests planned by parents, schools and
SNAs that were due to take place in cities and towns across the country tomorrow, including
outside Leinster House. The planned cuts were also the subject of a Sinn Féin Doyle
motion due to be debated this evening. A spokesperson for the Department of Education confirmed
that the 19 million euro to fund this significant shift is additional funding for the department
over and above its current budgetary allocation. Sinn Féin said the decision was a reprieve
for schools, families and SNAs, but it said the fundamental issues at the heart of SNA
provision policy remained unaddressed.
Ukraine is marking the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion with a series
of events to commemorate the start of the most devastating conventional conflict in
Europe since World War Two. According to the United Nations, 15,000 Ukrainian civilians
have been killed as a result of the Russian invasion, with hundreds of thousands of soldiers
on both sides thought to have been killed or injured. From the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv,
our Europe editor, Tony Connolly.
At 4.15am, Russia launched a full-scale land invasion of Ukraine. Columns of tanks poured
across the border along three main axes. There was an aerial bombardment from land, sea and
air. Vladimir Putin had expected a swift victory. Ukrainian intelligence later reported his
intention was to execute the democratically elected leadership of Ukraine and install
a pro-Russian government. However, Russia's attempt to capture Kyiv faltered. By that
summer, Russian troops had retreated to the east and were routed in Kherson and Kharkiv.
Yet hopes of a spectacular Ukrainian victory were short-lived. President Putin ordered
a partial mobilisation, violently suppressed opposition at home and turned Russia into
a war economy. The invasion has settled into a grinding war of attrition, with the loss
of hundreds of thousands of lives. Drone superiority counts for more than infantry formations or
artillery strength. The return of Donald Trump to the White House created a new dynamic,
but Europeans, who've supported Ukraine financially and increasingly militarily, fear he's putting
more pressure on Kyiv to surrender land as part of a settlement than on Mr Putin, who
has escalated attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and residential areas. The
war today enters its fifth year. Tony Connolly, RTÉ News, Kyiv.
The Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence, Helen McEntee, will today seek government
approval for a new national maritime security strategy. It's aiming to strengthen protections
around undersea cables and energy connections in Ireland's waters amid growing geopolitical
tensions. Our political correspondent, Michail O'Ham.
The strategy is advocating that cooperation with neighbouring states and international
partners is stepped up in this area. This includes the UK and France, and there would
be continued engagement too with the EU and NATO, while closer links with the private
companies that own much of Ireland's offshore infrastructure would also be a priority.
And legislation will be brought forward to provide the defence forces with clear enforcement
powers at sea. Later this morning, the Taoiseach will join
a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing on the fourth anniversary of Russia's invasion
of Ukraine. Michail Martin is expected to reaffirm this country's unwavering support
for Ukraine and its commitment to a just and lasting peace.

in public office. The 72-year-old former Labour minister is being investigated over allegations
he passed sensitive government documents to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein
while serving as business secretary. Earlier this month, police conducted searches of Mr
Mandelson's homes in London and Wiltshire. A total of ten transatlantic flights have
been cancelled today due to adverse weather conditions on the east coast of the United
States. The flights affected are to and from New Jersey, Boston and New York.

updated in the period ahead, also the workforce plan and a redeployment scheme.

So what you're seeing there is a fairly lengthy discussion process I think but
while nothing happens in the next school year, I suppose there is the
possibility of something further down the line but only after there's
agreement on those three points.

everything as it was, which became politically inevitable I think given the

powers and clearer definitions when it comes to the work and the enforcement
that they can carry out at sea. But I think overall, probably more lengthy and
extensive legislation will be required and that will take some time longer and
that would underpin the whole strategy.
Plans to speed up the building of large infrastructure projects also being

Yeah, this is happening quite a bit now, Justin, where the Minister for Public

cutting red tape essentially to get big projects delivered quickly.
This time it's about potentially reducing the number
of regulations that it's felt are impeding the delivery of things by up to

special ed policy and mainstream classes. In relation to the money that's

recruitment process. So you're expecting then from next September those nearly
200 schools who were recently told they would lose some of their SNAs that they

redeployment scheme in place. There's still a need to highlight the problem

confidence in the work of the NCSE. So I think the protests will probably go
ahead to highlight those issues. Thank you very much indeed Andy Pike, head of
